sections.description: Summarizes the patient’s symptoms, exam, and initial labs to frame the key problems and immediate priorities in an older man with fever, headache, mucocutaneous lesions, and hyponatraemia.
subtopics: Symptom constellation and time course: fever, headache, malaise, vertigo, hiccups, arthralgia, oral aphthae
Vital signs and focused exam: tachycardia, febrile, mucocutaneous lesions, clinically euvolemic status
Key initial laboratory abnormalities: hypotonic hyponatraemia, elevated CK, transaminitis, markedly elevated CRP/ESR, hyperglycaemia
Problem list: suspected CNS inflammation, newly recognized systemic inflammatory disease, euvolemic hypotonic hyponatraemia
Immediate diagnostic and safety priorities: exclude life-threatening CNS infection, assess sodium severity and symptoms, establish volume status, initiate targeted labs and imaging
Clinical clues to profound hyponatraemia: persistent hiccups, malaise; screen for rhabdomyolysis with CK

sections.section_title: Behçet’s disease and acute neuro-Behçet’s disease: focused background
sections.description: Provides the essential pathophysiology and diagnostic framework for BD and its acute neurological involvement relevant to this case.
subtopics: International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease (ICBD): point system, high specificity of genital aphthosis, role of pathergy test, HLA-B51 as supportive but non-diagnostic
Neuro-Behçet’s phenotypes: parenchymal (brainstem/diencephalon), non-parenchymal (e.g., cerebral venous thrombosis), and aseptic meningitis presentations
Typical investigations: early MRI may be normal; CSF often shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein; IL-6 frequently elevated in acute neuro-BD
Epidemiology and timing: neuro-BD in 10%–20% of BD patients, usually years after BD onset; concurrent BD and neuro-BD is uncommon
Clinical triggers to suspect neuro-BD: new headache, vertigo, meningitic symptoms, behavioral change, or focal deficits in a patient with mucocutaneous BD features

sections.section_title: Hyponatraemia and SIADH in neuroinflammation: mechanisms and diagnostic framework
sections.description: Explains SIADH pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, and its relationship to CNS inflammatory states like acute neuro-BD.
subtopics: SIADH diagnostic criteria and application: hypotonic hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine, elevated urine sodium, clinical euvolemia, normal thyroid/adrenal function; ADH level not required but may be elevated
Mechanistic link between CNS inflammation and ADH release: cytokine-driven (notably IL-6) hypothalamic stimulation and reset osmostat concepts
Differential diagnosis of hyponatraemia in this context: hypovolaemia, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, medications, pseudohyponatraemia; correct sodium for hyperglycaemia
Clinical manifestations and complications: nausea, gait issues, seizures; persistent hiccups as a clue; rhabdomyolysis as an under-recognized complication
Principles of safe correction: fluid restriction first-line, targets for rate of correction, monitoring to prevent osmotic demyelination

sections.section_title: Stepwise diagnostic workup and reasoning toward acute neuro-BD with SIADH
sections.description: Details how clinicians progressed from broad differentials to a unifying diagnosis by integrating clinical features, imaging, CSF, and serology while avoiding diagnostic pitfalls.
subtopics: Infectious evaluation for meningoencephalitis: CSF cell count/protein/glucose, cultures, HSV/VZV testing, cryptococcal antigen, TB studies; rationale for empiric acyclovir and de-escalation
Neuroimaging strategy: MRI can be normal early in neuro-BD; when to repeat or expand imaging if symptoms evolve
Excluding malignancy and other inflammatory mimics: CSF cytology, serum sIL-2R, ACE/lysozyme, and their limited specificity and sensitivity
Establishing BD diagnosis: applying ICBD points from mucocutaneous lesions; ophthalmologic assessment; pathergy test optional; HLA-B51 as non-essential supportive data
Integrating data: aseptic meningitis without MRI lesions plus mucocutaneous BD features supports acute neuro-BD; concurrent labs fulfill SIADH criteria
Test stewardship: targeted testing guided by clinical features to avoid over-interpretation of non-specific markers

sections.section_title: Management: treating acute neuro-BD and SIADH, monitoring, and when to escalate
sections.description: Outlines therapeutic decisions in this case, contrasts them with guideline-based standards, and specifies monitoring and escalation strategies.
subtopics: Initial empiric therapy during diagnostic uncertainty: broad-spectrum antibiotics and acyclovir; criteria for discontinuation once infections are excluded
Standard acute neuro-BD therapy: indications for high-dose corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents; when to involve immunology/rheumatology and neurology
Colchicine in BD: mechanism (neutrophil inhibition, cytokine modulation), dosing considerations, common adverse effects, drug interactions; evidence base and when monotherapy may be reasonable
SIADH management: fluid restriction thresholds, indications for hypertonic saline, role of salt tablets/urea or vaptans, targets for correction (<8–10 mmol/L in 24 h; lower in high-risk patients)
Monitoring response and safety: serial sodium and osmolality, urine studies, neuro checks, CK for rhabdomyolysis, inflammatory markers, medication adverse effects
Comorbidity considerations: interpret sodium with hyperglycaemia correction; long-term diabetes optimization to reduce confounders

sections.description: Summarizes the patient’s clinical course and distills actionable lessons, prognostic issues, and knowledge gaps.
subtopics: Case outcome: rapid improvement after colchicine, normalization of sodium and ADH, CK recovery, no corticosteroids used, sustained remission over years
Prognosis in acute neuro-BD: relapse risk, need for long-term follow-up and triggers for re-imaging or CSF reassessment

Clinical pearls: MRI may be normal early; SIADH can herald CNS inflammation in BD; do not over-rely on HLA-B51; watch for delayed appearance of genital ulcers; recognize hiccups and rhabdomyolysis as hyponatraemia clues
Knowledge gaps and future directions: IL-6–ADH axis in neuro-BD, defining when colchicine monotherapy suffices, registries/trials to refine treatment pathways
